title: CS6460 Module 3 · Scene quiz
note: Audit bank: lecture scenes → paraphrase choices (not vocab titles). Built from Module 3 lesson claims + practice-pool patterns. Not Canvas stems.

items.stem: Shulman already had content and pedagogy interlocking. Mishra and Koehler's TPACK move adds which foundational domain?

choices.text: Technological Knowledge — a third base domain that also creates new intersections with content and pedagogy.
Classroom Context Knowledge — a fourth domain sitting beside the original three.
A single unified teacher-skill score that replaces Pedagogical Content Knowledge.
Nothing new; they only renamed Pedagogical Content Knowledge.

items.explain: TPACK = Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge. Extends Shulman by adding TK as a third foundational domain.

items.stem: A algebra class uses Desmos so students drag parameters and watch the graph rewrite live. Why is that more than a faster chalkboard?

choices.text: The technology changes how the content can be represented and how instruction can be designed.
Any demonstration repeated across spaced sessions raises retention the same way.
The only gain is cutting the extraneous load of drawing neat axes by hand.
Immediate feedback always beats delayed teacher feedback, full stop.

items.explain: Joyner's Desmos example: qualitative change in representation and pedagogy, not mere efficiency.

items.stem: Designers choose between a narrated plate-tectonics video and a drag-the-plates simulation. Which review question most directly exercises technological content knowledge?

choices.text: Which option changes what aspects of the content are foregrounded and what questions get easy to ask?
Which option stays inside the team's production budget this year?
Which option keeps learners in the zone of proximal development?
Which option imposes less extraneous load on a first-time learner?

items.explain: TCK = how tech shapes what content is expressible/askable. Budget is TK/logistics; ZPD/load are nearby but not TCK.

items.stem: In Joyner's own cut, what actually marks a challenging driving question?

choices.text: Whether there is a single right answer responses can be judged against.
Whether the question grows out of the students' local community.
Whether answering it requires more than one subject area.
Whether it can realistically be finished in the time available.

items.explain: Instructor voice: challenging driving questions have better/worse answers, not one keyed correct answer.

items.stem: Why does the project/problem-based lesson treat collaboration as a core feature, not a convenience?

choices.text: Peers supply support inside the zone of proximal development.
Groups mainly let strong students demonstrate procedures for weak ones.
Groups exist so the public product can look larger to an audience.
Groups exist so each member can specialize and never integrate.

items.explain: Vygotsky ZPD framing: peers are a powerful source of support between alone-ability and with-help ability.

items.stem: Students spend six weeks producing historical documentaries; the graded assessment is a 40-item multiple-choice test afterward. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Treat the documentaries and successive drafts as the evidence of learning.
Keep the MC test and add a short reflection to consolidate.
Keep the MC test but delay it two weeks for spacing.
Keep the MC test but allow open notes.

items.explain: If the project is the learning work, assess that work — not a mismatched later MC proxy.

items.stem: Who introduced the concept of backward design, and in what work?

choices.text: Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe, in Understanding by Design (1998).
Ralph Tyler, in Basic Principles of Curriculum and Instruction (1949).
Jerome Bruner, in The Process of Education (1960).
Benjamin Bloom and colleagues, in the taxonomy of cognitive objectives.

items.explain: Wiggins & McTighe 1998 UbD introduced backward design. Tyler/Bruner/Bloom appear nearby as other curriculum frameworks.

items.stem: Joyner notes his own course covers assessment last — the wrong order under backward design. How does he frame that?

choices.text: As a trade-off: a more motivating sequence accepted instead of a slightly more effective one.
As proof that sequence barely matters for adult professionals.
As evidence that backward design only applies to K-12.
As an inherited error a later revision will quietly fix.

items.explain: Explicit trade-off language in the curriculum lesson: motivation over slight effectiveness gain.

items.stem: A platform team delivers an ordered list of thirty topics with time estimates and calls it the course design. Strongest objection from the curriculum lesson?

choices.text: A list of topics is not a curriculum; decisions about depth and path are missing.
Thirty topics exceed working-memory limits, so shorten first.
Reorder so the most engaging topics come first.
Check state standards before any building begins.

items.explain: Joyner: curriculum is architecture, not inventory.

items.stem: Which statement best matches Mayer's spatial contiguity principle?

choices.text: Corresponding words and images should be near each other on the page or screen rather than separated.
Corresponding narration and animation should play simultaneously rather than in sequence.
Complex lessons should be learner-paced segments rather than continuous.
Cues should highlight organization and key ideas.

items.explain: Spatial contiguity = nearness of words/images. Temporal contiguity, segmenting, signaling are sibling principles.

items.stem: Joyner groups Mayer principles into clusters. What most clearly separates his second cluster from the first?

choices.text: The first is about ruthless editing of wasted load; the second is about sequencing and pacing hard material.
The first is empirically supported; the second is speculation.
The first applies only to video; the second only to interactive software.
The first addresses intrinsic load; the second addresses only germane load.

items.explain: First cluster = cut/reorganize so WM is not wasted; second = structure arrival of genuinely complex content.

items.stem: A chart builds itself while a long explanatory paragraph sits beside it; learners cannot watch and read at once. Best Mayer-aligned fix?

choices.text: Move the explanation into spoken narration that plays while the chart builds.
Let learners choose either reading or watching, but keep both visual.
Show the paragraph first, then play the animation with no narration.
Shorten the paragraph and enlarge the typeface.

items.explain: Modality: graphics + spoken words beat graphics + on-screen text competing in the visual channel.

items.stem: What did David Rose and Anne Meyer do in the UDL story?

choices.text: Adapted Universal Design from architecture to education at CAST.
Founded the independent living movement and campaigned for curb cuts in Berkeley.
Established the social model of disability in academic disability studies.
Proved that matching instruction to modality preferences fails.

items.explain: Mace = architecture UD; Rose & Meyer at CAST = UDL. Roberts/Oliver/learning-styles myth are nearby names.

items.stem: Joyner names a third, most important difference between UDL and learning styles. What is it?

choices.text: UDL provides multiple representations to everyone rather than sorting learners into matched channels.
UDL applies only to assessment; learning styles apply only to delivery.
UDL routes each learner to the channel testing shows is best for them.
UDL was validated in RCTs; learning styles only in surveys.

items.explain: Do not sort; give everyone multiple means. Sorting is the learning-styles move UDL rejects.

items.stem: A PM refuses captions because under 2% of enrollees report a hearing impairment. Best lesson-backed reply?

choices.text: Captions serve many more learners than that survey group, as curb cuts did on the street.
Add captions only to the conceptually heaviest videos.
Captions matter only if a regulator is watching.
Skip captions; the survey already proves demand is tiny.

items.explain: Curb-cut effect: access features designed for one group often help almost everyone.

items.stem: On the Distributed Classroom space spectrum, what are the three positions?

choices.text: With the instructor; with a cohort but remote from the instructor; fully remote alone.
Main campus; official satellite; any location the student chooses.
Classroom; supervised testing center; unsupervised home.
With the instructor; watching a recording later; never engaging.

items.explain: Joyner & Isbell space axis: co-located with instructor; cohort-remote; fully remote alone.

items.stem: Why invest more in materials made for a distributed classroom?

choices.text: Content can outlive the class it was made for and reach audiences you cannot anticipate.
Higher production values reliably raise satisfaction scores.
Accreditation now grades production polish.
Well-produced media always cut the cost of every later term to near zero.

items.explain: Lesson: materials outlive the cohort — design and invest accordingly.

items.stem: An eight-week online program has weekly deliverables and staff review but cannot verify who did the work and cannot award credit. What can it legitimately offer?

choices.text: A certificate — completion with some structure and accountability, not academic credit.
Academic credit, because staff review counts as assessment.
Nothing beyond content access, ever.
Provisional credit that auto-converts later.

items.explain: Certificate ≠ credit. Credit needs institutional claim + verification rigor.

items.stem: In the running writing-assignment example, which description is Augmentation?

choices.text: Spell check, easy paragraph reorganization, and digital submit — same essay task with functional gains.
Typing instead of handwriting with nothing else changed.
Co-authoring a public multimedia document with peers abroad.
Drafting in a shared doc while peers comment in real time (task redesign).

items.explain: Substitution = type instead of write. Augmentation = functional improvement, same core task. Mod/Redef = redesign / previously impossible.

items.stem: How does the lesson divide labor between SAMR and TPACK?

choices.text: SAMR notices how modest or transformative the integration is; TPACK evaluates whether going further is a good idea.
They compete; pick one framework and ignore the other.
SAMR supersedes TPACK once a teacher is comfortable with tech.
TPACK only diagnoses modest use; SAMR judges pedagogical wisdom.

items.explain: Complementary: SAMR = degree of change; TPACK = whether the design works pedagogically.

items.stem: Stats goal: choose and justify a hypothesis test. Software could auto-select the test; instructor allows it only for arithmetic. Colleague wants Modification. Evaluate.

choices.text: The instructor is deliberately holding integration at the level that fits the learning goal.
Leaving the software's main capability unused always wastes the technology.
Always let the tool choose the test and reframe the goal around reading output.
Show only the final p-value to cut extraneous processing.

items.explain: Higher on SAMR is not always better; match level to the learning goal.

items.stem: In the Practical Inquiry Model, what is the integration phase?

choices.text: Making sense of ideas from exploration and building connections between them.
A sparking problem that starts curiosity.
Open brainstorming and idea-sharing without yet connecting.
Testing the constructed understanding against the original problem.

items.explain: Triggering → exploration → integration → resolution. Integration is where community helps most.

items.stem: Why does weak social presence make cognitive presence harder?

choices.text: Genuine integration needs honest discourse, which happens when people feel safe as real people.
Instructors simply lack prior-knowledge data in those environments.
Isolated learners always skip readings.
Anonymity mainly raises extraneous load while reading posts.

items.explain: Without social presence, learners avoid intellectual risk; integration stalls.

items.stem: Week three has ninety varied, thoughtful posts; nobody has tied them together and time is almost up. Best facilitating-discourse move?

choices.text: Name which threads connect and ask the group to reconcile them.
Post the correct answer so discussion can stop.
Only schedule a sync video for social presence and ignore the threads.
Cut the required post count so fewer people write.

items.explain: Facilitating discourse = guide interaction while it happens; weave, don't replace with the key.

items.stem: Most defensible ethical position on AI authorship for now, per the lesson?

choices.text: Transparency about what was generated, by what means, and what role human judgment played.
Treat AI output as public domain until copyright settles.
Ban any AI-touched work from academic credit.
Allow AI only on outputs learners never see.

items.explain: Lesson: for now, transparency is the most defensible stance while law catches up.

items.stem: Why is sociopolitical consciousness often the hardest of Ladson-Billings' three requirements?

choices.text: It asks educators to help students critique the systems they are also trying to succeed within.
It is the hardest to put on a standardized test.
Most teachers lack any cultural knowledge at all.
It always replaces academic success instead of sitting beside it.

items.explain: Academic success + cultural competence + sociopolitical consciousness; the third critiques the systems of success.

items.stem: A certificate grades every module with one timed oral, though the goal is disease-transmission reasoning. Strong written analyses, weak oral scores. Best response?

choices.text: Offer multiple means of demonstrating mastery — the format is incidental to the stated goal.
Keep one format so ranking stays fair.
Only add spaced oral practice so the format becomes familiar.
Add growth-mindset comments and leave the single format alone.

items.explain: Separate knowledge from format. Can't-show-it-this-way ≠ doesn't-know-it.
